Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.
A common type of ovarian cancer treated with surgery and chemotherapy.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. For certain conditions, such as mediastinal gray zone lymphoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer, it is a common or necessary treatment, though it is not highly effective against most thyroid cancers. In stem cell rescue procedures, high-dose chemotherapy is used to destroy lymphoma cells and bone marrow stem cells. Specific drug examples include platinum-based agents like cisplatin and carboplatin, as well as capecitabine and paclitaxel.

Because chemotherapy targets all fast-dividing cells, it can also harm healthy cells, leading to side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fever, infection, tingling or numbness, and rash. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility, as the treatment can affect fertility. Chemotherapy is considered a non-hormone therapy and is a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment, though its effectiveness and side effects depend on the specific drugs used and the individual patient's condition.
A common side effect of ovarian cancer surgery.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.
A common side effect of any surgery, including ovarian cancer surgery.

Platinum-Based Chemotherapy is a category of systemic therapy that utilizes platinum-containing drugs, such as cisplatin and carboplatin, to treat various types of cancer. This approach is frequently employed as a first-line or initial treatment for several malignancies, including ovarian cancer, where it serves as a primary therapeutic option. In the context of cervical cancer, platinum-based chemotherapy is the most commonly used systemic therapy, often applied to manage metastatic forms of the disease. Additionally, it is recommended for use in combination with radiation therapy for certain cases of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), enhancing the effectiveness of treatment. Beyond these applications, this chemotherapy class is also established as a first-line therapy for metastatic anal cancer. Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

The TNM System is a standardized cancer staging system used to describe the anatomical extent of a malignant disease. For each specific cancer, the T, N, and M scores are defined to reflect the unique patterns of local growth, lymphatic spread, and distant dissemination. Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures of the lymphatic system and integral components of the body’s immune system. Distributed throughout the body, they act as filters for lymph fluid and help fight infection. In the context of cancer, lymph nodes are significant because they can be primary sites of metastasis, where cancer cells spread from a primary tumor. Regional lymph nodes are those located near the tumor, and sentinel lymph nodes are specifically the first nodes to which cancer cells are expected to drain and spread. Cancer involvement in lymph nodes can cause them to swell, and this spread is often detected through imaging techniques such as PET/CT scans, as well as through biopsies. Because they are common sites of metastasis, lymph nodes are frequently biopsied to determine whether cancer has spread, which is a critical step in staging and treatment planning.

Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

Key points Being diagnosed with a brain tumor can be frightening and overwhelming. This book will help you make sense of all the information that’s out there. It will also describe your options for treatment. Taken together, you’ll have the confidence to make wellinformed decisions. What is primary CNS lymphoma? Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). After you’re infected, the virus remains dormant (inactive or “sleeping”) in your body for life. Although primary CNS lymphoma can occur at any age, the majority of people diagnosed with it are in their 60s or 70s. How is primary CNS lymphoma diagnosed? Other such symptoms may include changes in personality or behavior, depression, confusion, memory problems, loss of bladder control (incontinence), or difficulty speaking or swallowing. As the lymphoma tumor grows, it puts pressure on the CNS. This pressure often leads to neurological symptoms and difficulties, including headaches, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Key points Being diagnosed with a brain tumor can be frightening and overwhelming. This book will help you make sense of all the information that’s out there. It will also describe your options for treatment. Taken together, you’ll have the confidence to make wellinformed decisions. What is primary CNS lymphoma? Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). After you’re infected, the virus remains dormant (inactive or “sleeping”) in your body for life. Stages are categories that describe where the cancer has or hasn't spread from the ovary. Surgery is needed in order to know exactly how much cancer is in the body. When possible, a gynecologic oncologist should perform the initial surgery. This type of doctor is an expert in surgery and chemotherapy for gynecologic cancers. Your care team may also include a medical oncologist. This doctor is an expert in treating cancer with chemotherapy and other medicines. You may also receive care from registered nurses, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, social workers, genetic counselors, sexual health experts, and others. Ask for the names and contact information of your care providers to be included in the treatment plan. Cancer treatment may be improved if your primary care provider is involved. They can help manage other health conditions that may be affected by your cancer treatment. Your treatment plan There isn't one treatment plan that is best for everyone. There is often more than one option, including clinical trials. Clinical trials study the safety and effectiveness of investigational treatments. The treatment that you and your care team agree on should be noted in the treatment plan, along with possible side effects. Keep in mind that your plan may change. Testing may provide new information. Your feelings about treatment may change. Side effects or other health conditions may prompt a change of plan. Key points The ovaries are a pair of grapesized organs in the pelvis. They make hormones and eggs for sexual reproduction. Most ovarian cancers affect the layer of tissue surrounding the ovaries, called the epithelium. High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma are the most common types of ovarian tumors. Less common ovarian cancers can start in the epithelium, in tissues that support the ovaries, or in the reproductive (egg) cells of the ovary. Treating ovarian cancer takes a team of experts. Gynecologic oncologists and medical oncologists often work together to plan your treatment. 2 Testing for ovarian cancer Abdominal and pelvic exam Imaging tests Biopsy Family history and genetic testing Nutritional and digestive tract health Blood tests Biomarker testing Key points This chapter describes the testing used to learn more about suspected ovarian cancer, including whether surgery is possible. Ovarian cancer can cause changes in the body that you can feel or notice. But you might not have symptoms until the tumor has grown large or the cancer has spread. Common symptoms include: Feeling bloated Heartburn and indigestion Pain or pressure in the pelvis or belly Trouble eating or feeling full fast Having to urinate often or urgently Pain during sex These symptoms can also be caused by hormonal changes or other common health problems.

entities.description:
Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.
The return of cancer after treatment.<SEP>The return of cancer after treatment, considered in risk assessment.
A disease characterized by the growth of cancer cells in the ovaries, with stages and recurrence patterns.

Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Detection and risk assessment involve various tests, including PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, biopsy, and grading, and the disease often requires staging and treatment. The condition is also a focus of risk assessment and genetic testing discussions, as it is characterized by the presence of prostate cancer cells and abnormal cell growth within the gland.
A common type of ovarian cancer treated with surgery and chemotherapy.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed, cross-sectional pictures of areas inside the body, including organs, soft tissues, bones, and internal structures. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for repeated imaging. The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

In oncology, MRI plays a critical role in cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning. It is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement, notably in rectal cancer staging, and to detect cancer spread in the spine and brain. MRI is considered the most useful imaging test for identifying primary CNS lymphoma and gliomas, as it provides high-resolution images of the brain and spinal cord. For breast tissue examination, MRI helps detect abnormalities and can guide biopsies. Additionally, MRI is employed to guide applicator placement and design brachytherapy treatment plans, and it can be combined with computerized navigation systems to precisely guide biopsies. It is also used for further imaging of suspicious lymph nodes and for imaging surveillance, often with contrast, to monitor disease progression or recurrence. In some cases, MRI is combined with PET or CT to provide complementary anatomical and functional information, enhancing diagnostic accuracy across a range of clinical applications.
Ovarian cancer caused by inherited gene mutations, most commonly in BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes, or Lynch syndrome.

The return of basal cell skin cancer to the original area or spread to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body.<SEP>The return of cancer after treatment, also called relapse.<SEP>The return of cancer after treatment.<SEP>The return of cancer after treatment; risk is related to tumor grade.<SEP>The return of cancer after treatment, which surveillance aims to detect early.<SEP>The return of cervical cancer after treatment, or persistent cancer that does not improve.<SEP>The return of cancer after a cancer-free period.
Leg swelling is a common side effect of ovarian cancer surgery.

Targeted Therapy is a form of systemic cancer treatment that uses medicines or drugs to identify and attack specific molecules, genes, proteins, or receptors involved in the growth, spread, and survival of cancer cells. Unlike broad-spectrum treatments like chemotherapy, this approach focuses on particular genetic changes, mutations (e.g., PIK3CA), or biomarkers (e.g., PARP inhibitors) present in tumors, making it effective for cancers with certain molecular features. By targeting these specific parts of cancer cells, the therapy aims to slow or stop tumor progression, and it may potentially cause fewer side effects than chemotherapy, though it can also be combined with chemotherapy in certain contexts, such as for primary CNS lymphoma.

This therapy is applicable across various cancer types, including advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent and/or metastatic cervical cancer, and thyroid cancers that cannot be treated with surgery or radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy, have recurred, or have metastasized and continue to grow. For thyroid cancer, the targeted therapies currently used are kinase inhibitors, typically administered as swallowed capsules. However, the treatment is not without risks; side effects can include body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding, and some agents may adversely affect the heart, skin, and digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can impact fertility, and its use is often guided by biomarker testing to determine patient eligibility.

As a systemic therapy, it is generally reserved for cases where specific genetic targets are identified, and it may be employed when other treatments have failed or are unsuitable. The overarching goal remains to attack specific types of cancer cells while minimizing harm to normal cells, thereby offering a more precise treatment option for individuals with particular gene mutations or molecular profiles.

contexts: About basal cell skin cancer What is basal cell skin cancer? How is basal cell skin cancer treated? What can you do to get the best care? Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. Skin lesions Basal cell skin cancer is often found on the face, head, and neck. Here is a basal cell lesion pictured on a person's cheek. Skin basics Did you know that your skin is your body’s largest organ and if you measured it it would stretch to about 20 square feet? Working as a barrier, your skin protects you from bacteria and chemicals and helps control your body temperature. It has 3 layers: Epidermis – The top layer of skin provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis – The middle layer involves connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles. Hypodermis – The deepest tissue layer is made up of fat and connective tissue. Most skin cancers form in the cells of the epidermis. It has 3 main types of cells: Squamous cells – These cells are flat cells found in the upper part of the epidermis. Basal cells – Found in the lower part of the epidermis, basal cells constantly divide to form new cells that replace the squamous cells on the skin’s surface. Melanocytes – Melanocytes are cells located in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin. Melanin is responsible for our hair, skin, and eye color. It also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. This book is only about basal cell skin cancer. For more information on squamous cell skin cancer or melanoma, read the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Signs and symptoms Basal cell skin cancer can happen to anyone but it’s most common in people with lighter skin, lighter hair, or lighter eyes. In lighter skin, its lesions can look like any of the following: h Flat, pale or yellow areas, like a scar h Red patches that might be itchy Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas Open sores that don’t heal and might bleed, or go away and come back In darker (brown and black) skin, basal cell skin cancer can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border. It can be mistaken for a normal mole. Be sure to look out for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. Skin cancer is easier to cure when it is caught early. To find out how basal cell skin cancer is diagnosed, read Chapter 2: Testing for basal cell skin cancer. Causes and risk factors Basal cell skin cancer is caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or other sources like tanning beds. UV radiation can harm the DNA inside basal skin cells. DNA controls how cells grow and function. If the DNA inside cells becomes damaged, the cells can become abnormal and grow out of control. You’re more likely to have basal cell skin cancer if you have certain risk factors. A risk factor increases the chance of developing cancer. Risk factors for basal cell skin cancer include: UV light exposure – UV light (radiation) that comes from the sun or tanning beds increases your risk. Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color – People with lighter-colored skin are at a higher risk of developing skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. Age – Risk increases with age because sun exposure builds up over time. But skin cancer is becoming more common in younger people. History of skin cancer – If you or someone in your family has had skin cancer, you’re more likely to develop any type of skin cancer. Radiation therapy – Radiation treatment for other conditions, especially at a young age, can cause skin cancer. Immune suppression – People with weakened immune systems from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases are at higher risk for basal cell skin cancer. How is basal cell skin cancer treated? Basal cell skin cancer is highly treatable and curable. Catching it and treating it early is key. Surgery is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer. In some cases, radiation therapy or systemic therapy might be used to treat it. Following your treatment, you will have full skin exams with your doctor at least once a year. Between these periods, prevention is important. See Chapter 4: Treatment by risk and recurrence for more information. Recurrence is when basal cell skin cancer returns to the area where it was originally found, or it has metastasized (spread) to the lymph nodes or to distant parts of the body. But there are several options for how to treat it. Read more about how your cancer is treated in Chapter 3: Types of treatment and Chapter 4: Treatment by risk and recurrence. What can you do

NSCLC, found at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. What are the causes and risk factors? Smoking cigarettes is the main cause of SCLC. Almost everyone with SCLC smokes or has smoked. Many people with SCLC have regularly smoked more than a pack a day. Exposure to second-hand smoke also increases the risk of lung cancer. Secondhand smoke is the smoke exhaled by another person and the smoke from combustible tobacco products. Although rare in Western countries, there are occasions where people with no smoking history develop this disease. There are other unknown causes of SCLC. Researchers are still learning why some people who smoke never get lung cancer and others who have never smoked do. A person’s chances of getting SCLC are higher in the following situations: Over 70 years of age Prior radiation therapy to the chest Exposure to cancer-causing chemicals (also known as carcinogens), such as radon and asbestos If you don’t smoke, don’t start. If you do smoke, quit. New lung tumors are less likely to develop after quitting smoking. Nicotine addiction is one of the hardest addictions to stop. The stress of having cancer may make it even harder to quit. There is help. Ask your health care providers about counseling and medicines to help you quit. What are the symptoms of SCLC? SCLC can cause many types of symptoms. The symptoms depend on where the lung tumor has grown to or spread. SCLC can prevent the lungs from getting the air they need. Some people also have symptoms from paraneoplastic syndromes, which are caused by an abnormal body response to lung cancer. Some symptoms caused by SCLC are listed in Guide SCLC is often found when it’s causing symptoms or routine blood tests are abnormal. Less often, it’s found in x-rays or CT scans before symptoms start. Unlike other lung cancers, it’s difficult to detect SCLC early because it grows more quickly. Airways of the lungs Air moves through your body in a series of airways. It travels down your throat and through the windpipe (trachea). The windpipe splits into 2 airways called bronchi. Inside the lung, each bronchus branches off into the parts of the lung, called lobes. The right lung has 3 lobes, and the left lung has 2 lobes. The bronchi divide into smaller airways called the bronchioli. At the end of the bronchioli are sacs called alveoli. Oxygen is transferred from air into the blood in the alveoli. Your primary care provider may be the first to suspect that you have lung cancer. You will need to see specialists to determine if you have cancer. Your assessment team may include the following board-certified experts: Thoracic radiologist Interventional radiologist Pulmonologist Thoracic surgeon Medical oncologist Radiation oncologist To confirm that you have cancer, you’ll need testing of your body tissue or fluid. Small samples will be removed from your body during a procedure called a biopsy.

Key points Small cell lung cancer forms from cells that line the inner airways of the lungs. It’s a cancer that can be aggressive and grows fast. This chapter gives you the basics of small cell lung cancer. What is lung cancer? The lungs are the main organs of the respiratory system. They deliver oxygen to the blood and remove carbon dioxide from the blood. The transfer of these gases in and out of the body is called respiration. Lung cancers form from cells that line the airways of the lungs. The lungs' airways are called the bronchus, bronchioli, and alveoli. Cancer cells don’t behave like normal cells. They break the rules of cell growth. Cancer cells make many new cancer cells. They also do not die when they should. This overgrowth of cancer cells becomes a mass of tissue called a tumor. Cancer cells grow out of control. They can grow through the airway and into the lung tissue. They can grow through the lung wall and invade other body parts. Cancer cells can break away from a tumor and spread. They can enter the bloodstream or a fluid called lymph and spread to other places. This out-of-control cell growth can harm the body. Cancer cells crowd out and overwhelm normal cells. Without enough normal cells, cancer cells can cause organs to stop working. Scientists have learned a great deal about cancer. As a result, today’s treatments work Small cell lung cancer cells appear small and blue when viewed with a microscope. better than treatments in the past. Also, many people with cancer have more than one treatment option. When viewed with a microscope, SCLCs appear small and blue. Sometimes lung tumors contain both small cell and non-small cell lung cancer cells. These are called combined (small and non-small) cell lung carcinomas and are usually treated like small cell lung cancer. SCLC is much less common than NSCLC. It is the focus of this book. Smoking cigarettes is the main cause of SCLC. Almost everyone with SCLC smokes or has smoked. Many people with SCLC have regularly smoked more than a pack a day. Exposure to second-hand smoke also increases the risk of lung cancer. Secondhand smoke is the smoke exhaled by another person and the smoke from combustible tobacco products.

Family History is a comprehensive record of the health information of an individual's blood relatives, including parents, siblings, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and half-siblings. This information encompasses the presence of various diseases and health conditions, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, along with the age at which relatives were diagnosed. It serves as a critical tool in clinical practice, used to assess an individual's risk for inherited conditions and to guide healthcare decisions, treatment plans, and preventive care.

The utility of Family History is particularly pronounced in oncology. It is a key risk factor for several types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, thyroid cancer, and bladder cancer. For instance, having a close relative (like a parent or sibling) with prostate or bladder cancer increases an individual's chance of developing the disease. Furthermore, a detailed history of cancer occurrences in family members, including the specific type of cancer and age of onset, is essential for identifying potential hereditary cancer syndromes. This information can prompt healthcare providers to recommend genetic testing and risk assessment to determine if an individual carries a higher genetic predisposition for certain malignancies, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, also referred to as CSCC, is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells in the skin. It is the second most common form of skin cancer and is highly treatable, particularly when detected early. The condition is most often caused by cumulative sun exposure, and it can also develop in areas of skin that have been damaged by ultraviolet radiation. In addition to sun-damaged skin, CSCC can form in scars, chronic wounds, old burns, or other areas of prior skin injury; cases arising in such contexts may be more challenging to treat.

The disease has the potential to spread, or metastasize, to lymph nodes and other parts of the body, which underscores the importance of timely intervention. Treatment options for squamous cell skin cancer include topical therapies and surgical removal, with the choice of approach depending on the lesion's characteristics and location. The condition encompasses various subtypes, and risk factors—such as history of skin damage or chronic inflammation—are important considerations in its development and management. Overall, while CSCC is a serious malignancy, its prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate and prompt care.

It is classified as a type of head and neck cancer and most commonly originates in the squamous cells, making it typically a squamous cell carcinoma of the mucosa of the lip and other oral surfaces. The disease is a recognized topic in medical literature and is referenced in resources such as the NCCN (National Comprehensive Cancer Network) guidelines, which provide further information on its management.

Clinically, Mouth Cancer is staged using the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system, with stages ranging from 0 to 4. This staging process is crucial as it directly guides treatment decisions, helping clinicians determine the appropriate therapeutic approach based on the extent of the disease. However, from a molecular perspective, testing for this cancer has limited value due to the scarcity of targeted drugs available for its treatment, which contrasts with other cancer types where molecular profiling may offer more actionable therapeutic options. Overall, Mouth Cancer encompasses a range of malignancies within the oral cavity, with its diagnosis, staging, and treatment protocols being well-documented in oncological practice.

entities.description: Ultrasound is a medical imaging technique that uses high-energy or high-frequency sound waves to create pictures of the inside of the body. It is a painless procedure that does not involve x-rays, making it safe for repeated use. The technology is versatile and can visualize various internal structures, including breast tissue, the thyroid and neck, and lymph nodes. It is often the first imaging test used for suspected ovarian cancer and is also commonly employed to evaluate and monitor thyroid nodules, as well as to guide biopsies, such as those of the prostate or lymph nodes. In specific applications, it is used in echocardiograms to examine the heart. The technique is particularly effective at showing small areas of cancer within lymph nodes and is a standard tool for guiding interventional procedures.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

Tumor staging Tumors come in different shapes and sizes. So it’s not easy to compare one tumor to another. To solve this problem, cancer experts created the tumor, node, metastasis (TNM) system to describe any tumor. It’s based on the results of your imaging scans, biopsies, and blood tests. In this system, the letters T, N, and M stand for different areas of cancer growth: T (tumor) – Describes the size of the main (primary) tumor and if it has grown outside the prostate N (node) – Identifies whether cancer has spread to lymph nodes M (metastasis) – Indicates if cancer has spread (metastasized) to parts of the body outside of the pelvis Your provider will assign a number to each letter, based on your test results. The higher the number, the larger the tumor (T) or the more the cancer has spread (M). These scores are combined to assign a “stage” to the cancer. Staging is a way to describe how much cancer is in your body and how far it has spread. Knowing your stage is important for predicting the course of your disease and for making a treatment plan. Cancer staging is done when you’re first diagnosed. It may also be done after treatment to confirm that the stage hasn’t changed. How to read a TNM score Let’s say your prostate cancer is given a TNM score of T4, N1, MThis score means that the tumor has grown outside the prostate gland (T4) and has spread to nearby lymph nodes (N1) and to one or more distant parts of the body (M1). Why know your TNM score? For one, it lets you know the extent of your cancer. It also helps characterize your risk for the cancer to spread. Your level of risk helps indicate the most appropriate treatment for you. Measurements and assessments not covered in this book include PSA density, Gleason score, Grade Group, and risk groups. To learn more about these, see the NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Early-Stage Prostate Cancer, which can be found at NCCN.org/ patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. What’s next? After you’ve had all these tests to confirm you have prostate cancer, your care team will discuss your test results and will work with you to develop a plan for treatment. The next chapter describes the different treatment options for advanced-stage prostate cancer. After that chapter, you’ll read about which of those treatments may be right for you and your particular type of cancer. Key points Tests are used to plan treatment and check how well treatment is working. An unusually high amount of PSA in the bloodstream may be a sign of prostate cancer. Imaging tests are used to see where the cancer has spread beyond the prostate. Imaging also shows the size and location of the cancer. A biopsy is a procedure that removes samples of cells or tissue, which are tested for cancer. A genetic test is used to find abnormal changes (mutations) in your genes. An inherited genetic mutation occurs in every cell in your body. A somatic mutation occurs all by itself and is only found in the cells of a tumor. To find out if you have an inherited risk for cancer, talk to your doctor about germline testing or ask to be referred to a genetic counselor. 3 Prostate cancer treatments Hormone therapy Non-hormone therapy Clinical trials Supportive care What’s next? Key points There’s more than one treatment for advanced prostate cancer. This chapter describes the available treatment options and what you might expect from them. Talk with your care team about which treatment could be best for you. Prostate cancer is a complex disease with many treatment options. Treatments for advanced-stage prostate cancer include hormone therapy as well as non-hormone therapies like chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, and radiation therapy. Often, hormone therapy is combined with one or more other therapies. Combining therapies can be more effective than using either therapy alone. key word in ADT is “deprivation”—this therapy “deprives” (starves) the cancer of its main fuel: androgens. This can shrink the tumor or slow tumor growth for a while. You might hear the term “castration” used when describing prostate cancer or its treatment. This term describes a drastic reduction of testosterone. Castration can be done with hormone-lowering medication or by surgical removal of one or both testicles (orchiectomy). Though orchiectomy is a surgical procedure, it’s still considered hormone therapy because it removes the primary source of testosterone: the testicles. While drug hormone therapy can be reversed when the medication is stopped, orchiectomy is permanent and can’t be reversed. A hormone is a natural chemical made by a gland in the body. Its job is to activate cells or organs. Male hormones are called androgens. The main androgen is testosterone. Most of the testosterone in the body is made by the testicles. Testosterone helps produce sperm, among other functions. But testosterone also helps prostate cancer grow. A type of hormone therapy called androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) can stop your body from making testosterone or block cancer cells from using testosterone. The What is ADT? Adrenal glands produce hormones that affect your body in different ways. This chapter reviews the basics of adrenal tumors. Adrenal glands Your body has 2 adrenal glands. They are located on top of each kidney. Adrenal glands are small, yellow glands that are important to the body’s endocrine system. The endocrine system is made up of tissues and organs that produce hormones. Hormones are chemical substances that are made in one part of the body and carried through the bloodstream to other parts of the body where they help control how organs or cells work. Each adrenal gland has 2 main parts: Adrenal cortex – This is the outer part of the adrenal gland. The adrenal cortex makes 3 main hormones: cortisol, aldosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). These hormones control metabolism, blood pressure, and body features (such as hair growth and body shape). Adrenal medulla – This is the inner part of the adrenal gland. The medulla makes 3 hormones: epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. These hormones control the body’s response to stress. This includes the “fight or flight” surge of adrenaline. Adrenal glands Adrenal glands are small, triangle-shaped glands found on the top of the kidneys. These glands make hormones that help to regulate your immune system, response to stress, metabolism, and other functions. Functional adrenal tumors are usually benign, although some are capable of becoming cancerous and spreading. Benign functional tumors can still produce hormones and may be found during tests for hormone-related symptoms. Malignant adrenal tumors are cancerous tumors. Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

The TNM System is a standardized cancer staging system used to describe the anatomical extent of a malignant disease. It evaluates three key components: the primary tumor (T), the involvement of regional lymph nodes (N), and the presence of distant metastasis (M). These categories are assessed and combined to assign an overall cancer stage, which helps guide prognosis and treatment decisions.

This system is applied across various cancer types, including mouth cancer, throat cancer, and most bone cancers. For each specific cancer, the T, N, and M scores are defined to reflect the unique patterns of local growth, lymphatic spread, and distant dissemination. The TNM System provides a common language for clinicians to describe tumor size, extent of spread, and the presence of secondary growths, ensuring consistent and objective disease classification.

Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Targeted Therapy is a form of systemic cancer treatment that uses medicines or drugs to identify and attack specific molecules, genes, proteins, or receptors involved in the growth, spread, and survival of cancer cells. Unlike broad-spectrum treatments like chemotherapy, this approach focuses on particular genetic changes, mutations (e.g., PIK3CA), or biomarkers (e.g., PARP inhibitors) present in tumors, making it effective for cancers with certain molecular features. By targeting these specific parts of cancer cells, the therapy aims to slow or stop tumor progression, and it may potentially cause fewer side effects than chemotherapy, though it can also be combined with chemotherapy in certain contexts, such as for primary CNS lymphoma.

This therapy is applicable across various cancer types, including advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent and/or metastatic cervical cancer, and thyroid cancers that cannot be treated with surgery or radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy, have recurred, or have metastasized and continue to grow. For thyroid cancer, the targeted therapies currently used are kinase inhibitors, typically administered as swallowed capsules. However, the treatment is not without risks; side effects can include body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding, and some agents may adversely affect the heart, skin, and digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can impact fertility, and its use is often guided by biomarker testing to determine patient eligibility.

As a systemic therapy, it is generally reserved for cases where specific genetic targets are identified, and it may be employed when other treatments have failed or are unsuitable. The overarching goal remains to attack specific types of cancer cells while minimizing harm to normal cells, thereby offering a more precise treatment option for individuals with particular gene mutations or molecular profiles.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of blood cancer that starts in the stem cells of bone marrow. There are many subtypes of AML found in adults. This chapter will provide an overview of AML. What is AML? In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), abnormal changes stop very immature white blood cells called myeloid blasts or myeloblasts from becoming mature blood cells. As a result, there is a buildup of blasts in the bone marrow and blood. In turn, there are not enough healthy red blood cells, platelets, and white blood cells. This causes serious health issues. For this reason, AML is fatal if left untreated. Subtypes of AML There are many subtypes of AML. They are grouped and treated based on the presence or absence of certain gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes and other factors. In addition to AML, this book includes information about the following: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) Why you should read this book Making decisions about cancer care can be stressful. You may need to make tough decisions under pressure about complex choices. The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are trusted by patients and providers. They clearly explain current care recommendations made by respected experts in the field. Recommendations are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers. Cancer care is not the same for everyone. By following expert recommendations for your situation, you are more likely to improve your care and have better outcomes as a result. Use this book as your guide to find the information you need to make important decisions. What is blood? AML is a type of blood cancer. Blood is a tissue. A tissue is a group of cells that work together to perform a function. Blood’s function is to move oxygen and nutrients throughout your body and carry away waste. Blood also plays an important role for the immune system and in preventing bleeding. There are 4 main components of blood—plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Types of blood cells Your blood contains different types of cells that float in plasma. Plasma is a clear, yellowish fluid made up of mostly water. There are 3 types of blood cells: Red blood cells (RBCs or erythrocytes) carry oxygen throughout the body. White blood cells (WBCs or leukocytes) fight infections. WBCs include granulocytes (or neutrophils), monocytes, and lymphocytes. Platelets (PLTs or thrombocytes) help control bleeding. How are blood cells formed? Bone marrow is the organ that creates blood in our body. It is the sponge-like tissue in the center of most bones. Inside your bone marrow are early blood-forming cells called blood (hematopoietic) stem cells. Stem cells multiply to maintain a supply throughout our lifetime. Some of these stem cells gradually develop into blood cells through a process called differentiation. At any given time, the bone marrow contains cells at various stages of development, from very immature to nearly mature. Once a blood stem cell fully develops into a red blood cell, white blood cell, or platelet, it is released into the bloodstream as needed. Blood cell formation All blood cells start as blood stem cells. A blood stem cell has to mature or go through many stages to become a red blood cell, white blood cell, or platelet. AML affects the myeloid progenitor cells, which develop into red blood cells, granulocytes (a type of white blood cell), and platelets. A blast is an immature white blood cell. Blasts are committed to becoming a type of blood cell. Myeloblasts mature into granulocytes also known as neutrophils. These are types of immune cells that help prevent and control infection. In AML, abnormal myeloblasts are found in the bone marrow or blood. These blasts crowd out other blood cells causing bone marrow or blood to not work as it should. What's in this book? entities.description: Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures of the lymphatic system and integral components of the body’s immune system. Distributed throughout the body, they act as filters for lymph fluid and help fight infection. In the context of cancer, lymph nodes are significant because they can be primary sites of metastasis, where cancer cells spread from a primary tumor. Regional lymph nodes are those located near the tumor, and sentinel lymph nodes are specifically the first nodes to which cancer cells are expected to drain and spread. Cancer involvement in lymph nodes can cause them to swell, and this spread is often detected through imaging techniques such as PET/CT scans, as well as through biopsies. Because they are common sites of metastasis, lymph nodes are frequently biopsied to determine whether cancer has spread, which is a critical step in staging and treatment planning.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell that forms a crucial part of the immune system, helping to fight and prevent infection and disease. They are found in the blood, lymph tissue, and throughout all organs of the body. There are three main types of lymphocytes: B lymphocytes (B cells), T lymphocytes (T cells), and natural killer cells. Lymphocytes develop from lymphoid progenitor cells and mature from lymphoblasts.

These cells are central to immune function and are also key to understanding several diseases. Lymphocytes can grow out of control and become cancerous, leading to conditions such as lymphoma, including Hodgkin lymphoma. Additionally, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) originates in lymphocytes, as this cancer starts in these white blood cells. The abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes is directly linked to the development of lymphoma.

White Blood Cells, also known as leukocytes, are the infection-fighting cells of the blood and a crucial component of the immune system. They are primarily responsible for defending the body against infectious diseases and foreign germs. These cells are derived from blood stem cells and are found circulating in the bloodstream as well as within the lymphatic system, where they act as infection-fighting cells in the lymph.

White blood cells are categorized into several main types, including granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are a specific and vital subtype of white blood cell. Because of their role in immunity, the antigens present on white blood cells serve as important biomarkers. Their concentration in the blood is a key health indicator, commonly measured as part of a Complete Blood Count (CBC) test.

The behavior and counts of white blood cells are clinically significant in various diseases. For instance, Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) originates in these cells, specifically in lymphocytes. Conversely, in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL), white blood cell counts are often found to be abnormally high.
