Key points Different tests are needed to find out whether you have a glioma and what type it is. Testing also suggests what kind of therapy is most appropriate for you. You’ll need a variety of tests to diagnose a brain tumor and to make a treatment plan. (If you’ve already had testing and received a glioma diagnosis, you can turn to Chapter 3 to read about your treatment options.) Testing begins with an examination of your general health and an evaluation of your symptoms. Bring someone with you to listen, ask questions, and write down the answers. Health and symptoms Your care team needs to have all of your health information. They’ll ask you about any health problems and treatments you’ve had. Be prepared to talk about any illness or injury you’ve had and when it happened. Tell your care team about any symptoms you have. Symptoms Each part of the brain has its own job to do. Different parts of the brain manage different parts of the body. Symptoms occur when an area of the brain doesn’t work properly. Symptoms are often related to the location of the tumor in the brain as well as the size of the tumor. Symptoms develop as the glioma grows against, or weaves itself into, a part of the brain. This growth can cause swelling (edema) in the brain tissue around the tumor. Sometimes a tumor blocks the flow of fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) in and around the brain. Some people with low-grade gliomas never have symptoms. Low-grade gliomas generally grow slowly and can develop for years before they’re diagnosed. High-grade gliomas can cause a range of symptoms. These gliomas can grow quickly, developing in months or weeks. However, symptoms can also be caused by medical problems other than tumors. So for the most accurate diagnosis, be sure to tell your provider and care team about any and all symptoms you’re having, even if the symptoms seem unrelated. Common symptoms include: Headaches – Headaches are very common and often the first symptom in people with a glioma. Headaches can be worse in the morning, wake you up in the middle of the night, and occur with nausea and vomiting. Seizures – Seizures are also frequent in people with brain tumors. Seizures are often an early sign of a glioma, especially in low-grade gliomas. Fatigue – Fatigue is another common symptom of a glioma. Fatigue can be debilitating, frequent, emotionally overwhelming, and not related to how much sleep you get or how much activity you do. However, physical activity or exercise can sometimes help. Nausea and vomiting – Nausea and vomiting can be caused by the tumor putting increased pressure on the brain. Problems with thinking and speech – Examples include confusion, memory loss, and speech difficulties. Weakness or problems moving – People with a brain tumor may have muscle weakness on one side of the body, or difficulty with walking or balance. Changes in personality or mood – Changes in behavior

Prognosis is the likely course and outcome of a disease, such as cancer, serving as a prediction or forecast of how the condition will progress and resolve. It is a central concept in guiding treatment decisions, as it provides an expectation of the disease's trajectory and eventual result. The determination of a prognosis is informed by multiple clinical factors, including cancer staging, which helps predict the likely path of the disease. Additionally, biomarker and genetic tests are used to refine the prognosis, offering a more precise understanding of the disease's probable behavior based on the tumor's molecular characteristics. In essence, prognosis synthesizes information from staging and laboratory tests to articulate the anticipated course and outcome of the illness.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Key points Pancreatic cancer is one of the most common cancers. It is a challenging cancer to treat, but treatment is improving. Experts are studying the best ways to treat pancreatic cancer and are developing new treatments. Read this chapter to learn the answers to some common questions about pancreatic cancer. What is pancreatic cancer? Pancreatic cancer starts in a large gland called the pancreas. The pancreas is part of the digestive system. It makes enzymes that break down proteins, fats, sugars, and starches in food. It also makes hormones called insulin and glucagon that control blood sugar levels. Pancreatic cancer affects cell growth. Pancreatic cancer cells make many new cancer cells and do not die when they should. The overgrowth of pancreatic cancer cells becomes a mass called a tumor. Pancreatic cancer cells also don’t stay in place and may grow into nearby body tissue. They may break away from a tumor, spread to other areas, and form more tumors. There are 2 main types of pancreatic cancer The more common type of pancreatic cancer forms from exocrine cells. Exocrine cells make and move digestive enzymes. Pancreatic adenocarcinomas form from exocrine cells that line the tube-like ducts of the pancreas. They are also called pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and are the focus of this book. Pancreas Sounds like PAN-kree-us. The pancreas is deep inside the body. It sits just below the liver and behind the stomach. In adults, the pancreas is about 6 inches long. Less often, pancreatic cancer forms from endocrine cells. Endocrine cells make hormones. Pancreatic cancer that forms from endocrine cells is called a neuroendocrine tumor. Information on pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors can be found at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the app NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer. What causes pancreatic cancer? Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

Lumbar puncture, also known as a spinal tap, is a medical procedure that involves inserting a needle into the lower back to remove cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for diagnostic testing. The primary purpose of this procedure is to collect a sample of CSF, which can then be analyzed in a laboratory. It is frequently used to check for the presence of leukemia cells in the central nervous system (CNS) and spinal fluid, as well as to detect other cancer cells that may have spread to the CNS. By examining the collected fluid, healthcare providers can identify abnormalities, confirm a diagnosis, or monitor the effectiveness of treatment for conditions affecting the brain and spinal cord. The procedure is performed by a trained medical professional and is considered a standard diagnostic tool in neurology and oncology.

The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Surgery is a broad medical term for procedures that involve physical intervention, typically through an incision, to treat disease, remove cancer or other tissue, or repair the body. In oncology, it is a fundamental treatment modality used to physically remove tumors, cancerous tissue, and sometimes nearby lymph nodes. As a treatment for various cancers, its application and feasibility depend on the cancer type, stage, and location. For instance, it is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer and a primary treatment for early-stage cervical cancer, often involving the removal of cancerous tissue. For ovarian cancer, surgery is frequently the initial treatment, often performed by a gynecologic oncologist, and is typically followed by chemotherapy and maintenance therapy; its success depends on tumor size and location. In prostate cancer, surgery involves removing the cancerous tissue, which may include the tumor or the entire prostate, and is an option even for advanced stages. For bladder cancer, the procedure can range from removing the tumor to removing the entire bladder, depending on the stage, and may also involve removing surrounding tissue. In breast cancer, surgery is used as an initial treatment, after which pathologic staging provides more accurate details, and may involve the removal of breast tissue for analysis.

Surgery is also a key treatment for several other malignancies. It is a treatment option for early or locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and for some people with stage 1, 2, or 3 pancreatic cancer to remove cancer from the body. For thyroid cancer, it is a standard treatment involving the physical removal of tissue, with targeted therapy used when surgery cannot be performed. It is a main treatment for glioma, involving tumor removal, and can be the sole treatment for grade 1 gliomas. For chondrosarcoma and other bone cancers, surgery is used to remove tumors. In anal cancer, surgery may be used to remove the anus if the disease does not respond to treatment or returns. However, surgery is not always possible or successful, such as for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), and it is not normally an option for primary CNS lymphoma due to associated risks. Additionally, surgery may have increased side effects for smokers, and staging after the procedure provides more accurate details about the disease.

What is primary CNS lymphoma? What causes primary CNS lymphoma? How is primary CNS lymphoma diagnosed? Can primary CNS lymphoma be cured? What’s next? Key points Being diagnosed with a brain tumor can be frightening and overwhelming. This book will help you make sense of all the information that’s out there. It will also describe your options for treatment. Taken together, you’ll have the confidence to make wellinformed decisions. What is primary CNS lymphoma? Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). But people with primary CNS lymphoma often have one or more of these risk factors: Having an immunodeficiency disorder, which is an illness that weakens the immune system’s ability to fight infections and diseases. Primary CNS lymphoma is frequently linked to HIV, the immunodeficiency virus that causes AIDS. Carrying the Epstein-Barr virus, which is the virus that causes mononucleosis (“mono”) and other illnesses. Epstein-Barr is one of the most common viruses in humans. Most people are infected with it. After you’re infected, the virus remains dormant (inactive or “sleeping”) in your body for life. Having an autoimmune disease, such as lupus, in which the immune system overreacts and attacks healthy tissues and organs. Having an organ transplant, which requires medications that suppress the immune system. This leads to a higher risk of infections. Being an older adult. Although primary CNS lymphoma can occur at any age, the majority of people diagnosed with it are in their 60s or 70s. How is primary CNS lymphoma diagnosed? Primary CNS lymphoma is often found when a person develops symptoms. A symptom is a feeling or problem that may be a sign of disease. Symptoms usually develop over several weeks. Primary CNS lymphoma can cause a variety of symptoms. Symptoms are often related to the lymphoma’s location in the central nervous system. The most common location is in the central part of the brain. A lymphoma located here may cause specific nerve changes such as leg or arm weakness, or problems with coordination or movement. This system plays a key role in fighting infections. The tonsils, thymus, spleen, and lymph vessels and nodes are parts of the lymph system (shown). There are hundreds of lymph nodes in the body, and many are in the neck, armpits, and groin. How is CLL treated? Treatment of CLL depends on your body. You may not need treatment right away. But treatment may be needed if your white blood cell count is rising rapidly, if you have low numbers of other normal blood cells (anemia, low platelets, or low neutrophils), if you have large or uncomfortable lymph nodes, or if you have symptoms listed above. Many treatment options are available and should be discussed with your doctor at your first visit and as your condition is followed. These range from pills you take every day to a combination of IV infusions and pills taken for a specific amount of time. You may live for years without needing treatment. If or when someone needs treatment can vary greatly from person to person. You may have a more intense or aggressive treatment plan if you develop Richter transformation, which is described later. This rare condition can lead to a more aggressive cancer called diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) or another cancer called Hodgkin lymphoma. Is there a cure for CLL? There is currently no cure for CLL, but you can get effective treatment so your blood cells will be mostly healthy ones and a full life is possible. This is a condition called minimal residual disease. We’ll describe this in a later chapter. Fertility preservation refers to the range of actions, methods, and processes undertaken to safeguard a person’s ability to have biological children in the future, most commonly discussed and implemented before cancer treatment that may impair fertility. This practice is centered on keeping reproductive options open for later in life, particularly for patients who are at risk of infertility due to medical interventions such as chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. The core objective is to protect or save eggs, sperm, or reproductive tissue so that individuals can potentially conceive biological children after their treatment concludes.

The specific techniques involved in fertility preservation include the collection and freezing of sperm or eggs, as well as more advanced procedures such as ovarian tissue banking and ovarian transposition. These methods are designed to enable future pregnancy by preserving reproductive cells or tissues prior to the start of cancer therapy. The process is typically discussed with patients before they begin treatment, ensuring that they are informed of their options and can make proactive decisions about their reproductive health. While the primary context is cancer care, the underlying principle of fertility preservation is broadly applicable to anyone seeking to maintain the possibility of having children later in life, whether due to medical reasons or personal choice.

Treatment Plan is a comprehensive, personalized strategy for treating cancer, developed by a multidisciplinary care team in collaboration with the patient. It is primarily determined by diagnostic results, including imaging studies, biopsies, and blood tests, which help establish the cancer's stage and grade. The plan is designed to guide the selection of the most appropriate therapy, taking into account critical factors such as the patient's performance status and personal preferences. Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Performance Status is a clinical measure of a patient’s ability to perform daily activities, reflecting their overall well-being, general level of fitness, and capacity for self-care. It is commonly evaluated using standardized scales, such as the ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) scale, which assigns a score to quantify a person’s functional capability. This assessment is widely used in cancer care, including in the context of follicular lymphoma (FL), where it informs treatment planning and helps guide therapeutic decisions. Performance Status serves as a key indicator for determining the appropriate level of treatment intensity and is also used to assess a patient’s eligibility for clinical trials. By evaluating how well a patient can manage ordinary day-to-day tasks, this metric provides clinicians with essential information to tailor care and predict a patient’s ability to tolerate specific interventions.

Physical Exam is a broad clinical procedure performed by healthcare providers to assess a patient's overall health status, detect signs of disease, and inform diagnosis and treatment decisions. It is a fundamental component of medical care, utilized in various contexts such as the diagnosis of basal cell skin cancer, testing for DCIS, determining the clinical stage before treatment, and serving as a surveillance method for stages 2 and 3 colon cancer. During oncology care, it is performed by an oncologist every 1 to 3 cycles of chemotherapy to monitor the patient's condition and is also used during surveillance to detect potential recurrence.

The examination typically involves checking vital signs, measuring height and weight, listening to the lungs and heart, and examining the eyes, ears, nose, and throat. Providers also palpate body parts to assess organs and feel for enlarged lymph nodes, particularly in the neck, underarms, and groin. Depending on the clinical context, the exam may include specific assessments, such as a breast examination to check for abnormalities or palpation of the abdomen and pelvis to detect masses or other issues. It may also involve evaluating body systems and functional status to gauge physical ability.

As a general health check, the physical exam is a routine method for checking the body for signs of disease and assessing overall physical condition. It is a versatile tool used by various team members to evaluate a patient's health, detect abnormalities, and guide subsequent medical actions.

Your team should communicate and work together to bring the best knowledge from each specialty. This is called multidisciplinary care. Depending on your diagnosis, your multidisciplinary team may include a dozen or more specialists and care providers: Your primary care doctor handles medical care not related to your cancer. Your primary doctor can help you express your thoughts about treatments to your cancer care team. A urologist is an expert in the urinary system and the male reproductive organs. An anesthesiologist gives anesthesia, a medicine so you don’t feel pain during surgery or procedures. Advanced practice providers are an important part of any team. These are registered nurse practitioners and physician assistants who monitor your health and provide care. Residents and fellows are doctors who are continuing their training, some to become specialists in a certain field of medicine. Nutritionists offer guidance on what foods or diet are most suitable for your particular condition. Psychologists and psychiatrists are mental health experts who help manage issues such as depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions that affect how you feel. Genetic counselors are experts who interpret how your family history may impact your treatment. Urine cytology Urine cytology is a lab test that analyzes your urine for any cancer or precancerous cells. You may receive a urine cytology test if you have blood in your urine. A urine cytology is done like other urine tests— you pee into a small plastic container. Or, your urologist may collect a sample of your urine during cystoscopy. Either way, the urine sample is sent to a lab for testing. At the lab, a pathologist (a doctor who examines cells and tissue to find disease) uses a microscope to look for any abnormal cells in your urine sample. If abnormal cells are found, it means that cancer may be located anywhere in the urinary tract. You’ll need a cystoscopy procedure to find out if it’s in the urethra or the bladder. If cancer isn’t found in the urethra or bladder, you’ll need imaging tests to investigate the ureters, kidneys, or other areas. This procedure uses a cystoscope, a tube with a camera and a light at the end, which is inserted into the urethra and through to the bladder. Cystoscopy may be done at your urologist’s office, a hospital, or a clinic. The procedure takes only a few minutes, doesn’t require general anesthesia, and you can go home afterward. During a cystoscopy You’ll lie on your back on an exam table. You may be positioned with your feet up and your knees apart. After lubricating your urethra (and possibly numbing it with an anesthetic gel), your urologist will slowly insert the cystoscope into the opening of the urethra. This opening is at the tip of the penis or just in front of the vagina. This may be uncomfortable at first but it shouldn’t be painful. The cystoscope will move through the urethra and into the bladder. The urologist will view a monitor that shows real-time images of the inside of the bladder. About thyroid cancer 5 The thyroid 6 Who is at risk? 7 Key points There are different types of thyroid cancer. Most are curable with the right treatment. When possible, surgery is recommended for most thyroid cancers. The thyroid The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck. It has 2 lobes, a right and a left. A thin piece of tissue called the isthmus connects the lobes. The thyroid makes hormones. These substances are essential for the body to function properly. They circulate in the blood and help regulate body temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, weight, and metabolism (how fast food becomes fuel for your body). The two main hormones made by the thyroid are thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). Together, these are often referred to simply as “thyroid hormone.” The thyroid uses a mineral from your diet called iodine to produce these hormones. Certain foods and iodized salt contain iodine. There are four pea-sized glands on the back of the thyroid gland. These parathyroid glands control the amount of calcium in your bloodstream. Thyroid gland The thyroid is a butterflyshaped gland in the lower front part of the neck. It makes hormones that control blood pressure, metabolism, and other body functions. Thyroid nodules Thyroid nodules are small, often round areas of abnormal growth within the thyroid gland. Most are not cancerous. Very small nodules usually can't be seen or felt. Your provider may be able to see or feel a large nodule while examining your lower neck. Most thyroid nodules don't cause symptoms. They are often found by imaging tests done for a different reason. Symptoms of a larger nodule could include: A visible lump in the neck Neck pain Voice changes Trouble breathing Problems swallowing Who is at risk? Those assigned female at birth are 3 times more likely to be diagnosed with a thyroid cancer compared to those assigned male at birth. Compared to other cancers, thyroid cancer is often diagnosed earlier in adulthood. It is the most common cancer in adults aged 18 to 33 years. For more information on cancer in this group, see NCCN Guidelines for Patients: Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer at NCCN. org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Anything that increases the chances of developing a disease is called a risk factor. The most well-known risk factors for thyroid cancer are described next. Most people with thyroid cancer have no known risk factors. Radiation exposure Anyone who has had radiation treatment to the head or neck in the past (to treat a childhood cancer, for example) is at increased risk of thyroid cancer. Contact with large amounts of radiation in the environment as a result of a catastrophic event also increases the risk of developing a thyroid cancer. Family history Most thyroid cancers are sporadic, meaning there is no clear cause or risk factor. Only a small number are hereditary, or the result of inherited gene mutations (changes). A personal or family history of thyroid cancer or a related syndrome may increase the risk of thyroid cancer. Syndromes related to thyroid cancer include familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), Carney complex, Cowden syndrome, and multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN). Cowden syndrome is also known as PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS). This inherited syndrome can cause follicular thyroid cancer, and other cancers and health problems. Tell your provider if you have a personal or family history of breast, endometrial, or colorectal cancer. Key points The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland in the neck. Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Breast Cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in breast tissue, most commonly originating in the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units, specifically within the ducts or lobules. The vast majority of breast cancers are carcinomas. This malignant disease can spread to surrounding tissue and other parts of the body, such as the lungs; when it metastasizes, it is still referred to as breast cancer.

The condition is frequently associated with germline mutations, particularly in the BRCA genes, and can be hereditary in approximately 1 out of 10 cases. A personal or family history of breast cancer may also be linked to an increased risk of developing other cancers, such as prostate cancer and thyroid cancer. Clinical discussions of breast cancer often focus on staging, prognostic factors, and the use of biomarker testing and tumor markers for diagnosis and management.

Cancer Stage is a medical classification that describes the extent of cancer in the body, often written with Roman numerals (e.g., I, II, III, IV). It serves as a standardized assessment of how far the cancer has likely spread from its original site, such as the ovary, and is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment plan for a patient. The staging system categorizes the disease based on whether cancer has remained localized or has metastasized; specifically, stages I, II, and III are considered non-metastatic, indicating that the cancer is confined to the primary site or has spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes, while stage IV denotes metastatic cancer, meaning it has spread to distant organs or parts of the body. This classification provides a clear framework for healthcare providers to evaluate the severity of the disease, guide therapeutic decisions, and communicate the prognosis, ensuring that the treatment approach is tailored to the specific progression of the cancer.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, also referred to as CSCC, is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells in the skin. It is the second most common form of skin cancer and is highly treatable, particularly when detected early. The condition is most often caused by cumulative sun exposure, and it can also develop in areas of skin that have been damaged by ultraviolet radiation. In addition to sun-damaged skin, CSCC can form in scars, chronic wounds, old burns, or other areas of prior skin injury; cases arising in such contexts may be more challenging to treat.

The disease has the potential to spread, or metastasize, to lymph nodes and other parts of the body, which underscores the importance of timely intervention. Treatment options for squamous cell skin cancer include topical therapies and surgical removal, with the choice of approach depending on the lesion's characteristics and location. The condition encompasses various subtypes, and risk factors—such as history of skin damage or chronic inflammation—are important considerations in its development and management. Overall, while CSCC is a serious malignancy, its prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate and prompt care.

Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

The breast The breast is an organ and a gland found on the chest. The breast is made of milk ducts, fat, nerves, lymph and blood vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. Behind the breast is the pectoral (chest) muscle and ribs. Muscle and ligaments help hold the breast in place. Breast tissue contains glands that can make milk. These milk glands are called lobules. Lobules look like tiny clusters of grapes. Small tubes called ducts connect the lobules to the nipple. The ring of darker breast skin is called the areola. The raised tip within the areola is called the nipple. The nipple-areola complex (NAC) is a term that refers to both parts. Lymph drains from breast tissue into lymph vessels and travels to lymph nodes near your armpit (axilla). Lymph is a clear fluid that gives cells water and food. It also helps to fight germs. Nodes near the armpit are called axillary lymph nodes (ALNs). The breast The breast is a glandular organ made up of milk ducts, fat, nerves, blood and lymph vessels, ligaments, and other connective tissue. Breast cancer Breast cancer starts in the cells of the breast. Almost all breast cancers are a subtype called carcinomas. Carcinomas are cancers that start in the cells that line the inner or outer surfaces of the body. There are different types of breast carcinoma, most of which arise in cells that make up the lining (epithelial cells) in the terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) of the breast. The most common types are either ductal or lobular. Anyone can develop breast cancer, including those assigned male at birth. Although there are some differences between those assigned male and those assigned female at birth, treatment is very similar for all genders. How breast cancer spreads Cancer cells don’t behave like normal cells. Cancer cells differ from normal cells in the following ways. Primary tumor Over time, cancer cells form a mass called a primary tumor. Invasive Cancer cells can grow into surrounding tissues. Invasive breast cancer is breast cancer that has spread from the milk ducts or milk glands (lobules) into the surrounding breast tissue or nearby lymph nodes. Metastasis Unlike normal cells, cancer cells can spread and form tumors in other parts of the body called metastases. In this process, cancer cells break away from the first (primary) tumor and travel through blood or lymph vessels to distant sites. Once in other sites, cancer cells may form secondary tumors. Cancer that has spread to a nearby body part such as the axillary lymph nodes is called a local metastasis. It might be referred to as local/regional disease or locally advanced. Cancer that has spread to a body part far from the primary tumor is called a distant metastasis. Breast cancer can metastasize almost anywhere but most commonly spreads to the bone (including spine), lungs, liver, brain, or distant lymph nodes. Breast cancer that has metastasized to other parts of the body is still called breast cancer. The terms “chemotherapy” and “systemic therapy” are often used interchangeably, but they are not the same. Systemic therapy works throughout the body and includes chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, endocrine therapy, and others. A mutation in this gene can lead to increased growth of cancer cells and resistance to various treatments. Alpelisib (Piqray) is an example of a PIK3CA inhibitor. Immunotherapy Immunotherapy is a type of systemic treatment that tries to re-activate the immune system against tumor cells. The immune system has many on and off switches. Tumors take advantage of "off switches." Two leading off switches are PD-1 and CTLAImmunotherapy can be given alone or with other types of treatment. An immunotherapy example is pembrolizumab (Keytruda). Endocrine therapy Endocrine therapy blocks estrogen or progesterone to treat hormone receptorpositive breast cancer. The endocrine system is made up of organs and tissues that produce hormones. Hormones are natural chemicals released into the bloodstream. There are 4 hormones that might be targeted in endocrine therapy: Estrogen is made mainly by the ovaries, and also by other tissues in the body such as the fat tissue. Progesterone is made mainly by the ovaries. Luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) is made by a part of the brain called the hypothalamus. It tells the ovaries to make estrogen and progesterone and testicles to make testosterone. LHRH is also called gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). Androgen is made by the adrenal glands, testicles, and ovaries. Hormones may cause breast cancer to grow. Endocrine therapy will stop your body from making hormones or it will block what hormones do in the body. This can slow tumor growth or shrink the tumor for a period of time. Ovarian suppression uses drugs to temporarily stop the ovaries from making hormones. It is achieved with drugs called LHRH agonists. Breast Cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in breast tissue, most commonly originating in the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units, specifically within the ducts or lobules. The vast majority of breast cancers are carcinomas. This malignant disease can spread to surrounding tissue and other parts of the body, such as the lungs; when it metastasizes, it is still referred to as breast cancer.

The condition is frequently associated with germline mutations, particularly in the BRCA genes, and can be hereditary in approximately 1 out of 10 cases. A personal or family history of breast cancer may also be linked to an increased risk of developing other cancers, such as prostate cancer and thyroid cancer. Clinical discussions of breast cancer often focus on staging, prognostic factors, and the use of biomarker testing and tumor markers for diagnosis and management.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Metastatic Cancer is a term used to describe cancer that has spread from its original (primary) site to other, distant parts of the body. This process of spread can involve various organs and tissues, with common distant sites including the lungs, liver, bones, and brain, as well as distant lymph nodes. The condition is often characterized as very advanced disease, and when cancer is identified as stage 4 at the time of diagnosis, it is considered metastatic from the outset. In specific contexts, such as esophageal cancer, the metastatic stage specifically denotes that the disease has spread to distant bodily locations. Metastatic Cancer is a term used to describe cancer that has spread from its original (primary) site to other, distant parts of the body. This process of spread can involve various organs and tissues, with common distant sites including the lungs, liver, bones, and brain, as well as distant lymph nodes. The condition is often characterized as very advanced disease, and when cancer is identified as stage 4 at the time of diagnosis, it is considered metastatic from the outset. In specific contexts, such as esophageal cancer, the metastatic stage specifically denotes that the disease has spread to distant bodily locations. Regardless of the primary tumor's origin, the defining feature of metastatic cancer is its presence in areas far removed from the initial site of development.

Targeted Therapy is a form of systemic cancer treatment that uses medicines or drugs to identify and attack specific molecules, genes, proteins, or receptors involved in the growth, spread, and survival of cancer cells. Unlike broad-spectrum treatments like chemotherapy, this approach focuses on particular genetic changes, mutations (e.g., PIK3CA), or biomarkers (e.g., PARP inhibitors) present in tumors, making it effective for cancers with certain molecular features. By targeting these specific parts of cancer cells, the therapy aims to slow or stop tumor progression, and it may potentially cause fewer side effects than chemotherapy, though it can also be combined with chemotherapy in certain contexts, such as for primary CNS lymphoma.

This therapy is applicable across various cancer types, including advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent and/or metastatic cervical cancer, and thyroid cancers that cannot be treated with surgery or radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy, have recurred, or have metastasized and continue to grow. For thyroid cancer, the targeted therapies currently used are kinase inhibitors, typically administered as swallowed capsules. However, the treatment is not without risks; side effects can include body aches, rash, high blood pressure, and abnormal bleeding, and some agents may adversely affect the heart, skin, and digestive system. Additionally, targeted therapy can impact fertility, and its use is often guided by biomarker testing to determine patient eligibility.

As a systemic therapy, it is generally reserved for cases where specific genetic targets are identified, and it may be employed when other treatments have failed or are unsuitable. The overarching goal remains to attack specific types of cancer cells while minimizing harm to normal cells, thereby offering a more precise treatment option for individuals with particular gene mutations or molecular profiles.

It is highly treatable and can often be cured. Squamous cell skin cancer is a common skin cancer, especially in fair-skinned people. It is the second most common type of skin cancer, after basal cell carcinoma. The third type—melanoma—is much less common than the other types but can be more aggressive. Because they do not behave like melanoma, basal cell and squamous cell skin cancers are often referred to as nonmelanoma skin cancers or keratinocyte carcinomas. Cancer that starts in a squamous cell is called a squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cells are found in the top layer of the skin. They can also be found in other areas of the body, such as the lungs, thyroid, and esophagus. These types are treated differently than cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell skin cancers often begin as scaly patches on the skin that can become solid and misshapen. This cancer is also called cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC). This patient guide is about squamous cell skin cancer only. The terms “squamous cell skin cancer” and “CSCC” are used interchangeably throughout this guide. Skin basics Your skin is the largest organ of the body. Skin protects you from invaders (such as microbes), helps control body temperature, and allows the sensations of touch, heat, and cold. Skin has 3 layers: Epidermis is the outermost (top) layer of skin that provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis contains connective tissue, hair follicles, and sweat glands. Hypodermis (subcutis) is the deepest layer, made up of fat and connective tissue. Skin cancers are often formed in the epidermis. There are 3 main types of cells in the epidermis: Squamous cells: These cells are thin, flat cells that look like fish scales, and are found in the tissue that forms the surface of the skin. Basal cells: These cells are found in the lower part of the epidermis, called the basal cell layer. Basal cells constantly divide to form new cells to replace the squamous cells that wear off of the skin’s surface. As these cells move up in the epidermis, they get flatter, eventually becoming squamous cells. Melanocytes: These cells are found in the top layer of skin. Melanin is produced in the melanocytes. Melanin is responsible for the color of our hair, skin, and eyes. In addition to providing color, melanin also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. People who work outdoors are also at higher risk. Because longterm sun exposure can lead to squamous cell skin cancer, it is more common in people who have spent more years in the sun. Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Breast Cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in breast tissue, most commonly originating in the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units, specifically within the ducts or lobules. The vast majority of breast cancers are carcinomas. This malignant disease can spread to surrounding tissue and other parts of the body, such as the lungs; when it metastasizes, it is still referred to as breast cancer.

The condition is frequently associated with germline mutations, particularly in the BRCA genes, and can be hereditary in approximately 1 out of 10 cases. A personal or family history of breast cancer may also be linked to an increased risk of developing other cancers, such as prostate cancer and thyroid cancer. Clinical discussions of breast cancer often focus on staging, prognostic factors, and the use of biomarker testing and tumor markers for diagnosis and management.

Family History is a comprehensive record of the health information of an individual's blood relatives, including parents, siblings, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and half-siblings. This information encompasses the presence of various diseases and health conditions, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, along with the age at which relatives were diagnosed. It serves as a critical tool in clinical practice, used to assess an individual's risk for inherited conditions and to guide healthcare decisions, treatment plans, and preventive care.

The utility of Family History is particularly pronounced in oncology. It is a key risk factor for several types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, thyroid cancer, and bladder cancer. For instance, having a close relative (like a parent or sibling) with prostate or bladder cancer increases an individual's chance of developing the disease. Furthermore, a detailed history of cancer occurrences in family members, including the specific type of cancer and age of onset, is essential for identifying potential hereditary cancer syndromes. This information can prompt healthcare providers to recommend genetic testing and risk assessment to determine if an individual carries a higher genetic predisposition for certain malignancies, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).
Medical interventions to treat breast cancer; more successful when cancer is found early.

Genetic Testing is a medical diagnostic process that analyzes DNA to identify inherited (germline) mutations, typically performed on normal tissue samples such as blood, saliva, cheek swabs, or urine. This form of testing is distinct from tumor mutation testing, as it focuses on determining whether an individual carries hereditary genetic changes that increase their risk for developing cancer. It is commonly used to detect mutations in BRCA genes and other cancer-related genes, and is recommended for all individuals diagnosed with ovarian cancer to guide clinical management.

The scope of genetic testing extends beyond hereditary risk assessment. In oncology, it is also utilized to analyze genetic changes and biomarkers within cancer cells—such as leukemia cells—to inform treatment decisions and prognosis. Additionally, genetic testing serves as a method to identify specific mutations linked to prostate cancer and other malignancies, helping to tailor therapeutic approaches. The test can be performed on various sample types, including blood, saliva, urine, or tumor tissue, depending on the clinical question.

Genetic testing is also valuable for identifying mutations that cause inherited cancer syndromes, and results are often relevant for family members, as knowing whether a relative has undergone testing can influence interpretation of one’s own results. Overall, genetic testing plays a critical role in cancer risk assessment, early detection, and personalized treatment planning across multiple cancer types.

entities.description: Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

This staging process is crucial as it directly guides treatment decisions, helping clinicians determine the appropriate therapeutic approach based on the extent of the disease. However, from a molecular perspective, testing for this cancer has limited value due to the scarcity of targeted drugs available for its treatment, which contrasts with other cancer types where molecular profiling may offer more actionable therapeutic options. Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

Biomarker Testing is a medical procedure used in oncology that analyzes biological molecules—such as DNA mutations, proteins, or other molecular features—found in tumor tissue, biopsy samples, or blood to inform cancer care. Also known as molecular testing or tumor profiling, it is performed to identify specific genetic alterations or protein expressions that indicate the presence or progression of cancer, thereby aiding in diagnosis and prognosis. The testing examines genes or their products to detect mutations and proteins that may suggest effective treatment options, helping to guide decisions on whether a patient is eligible for targeted therapies or immunotherapies.

The scope of biomarker testing is broad, encompassing various cancer types and specific markers. For instance, it is used to guide diagnosis and treatment in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and to assess risk and aggressiveness in prostate cancer by examining molecular components of biopsy samples. Common biomarkers tested include hormone receptors, HER2, PD-L1, MMR, MSI, TMB, NTRK, RET, p16, and EBV DNA, among others. These tests help determine the presence of specific biological markers that can predict response to particular drugs, thereby fine-tuning treatment plans and improving diagnostic accuracy.

Biomarker testing can be performed on tumor tissue or through liquid biopsies of blood, depending on the clinical need. The results provide critical information on the molecular profile of the cancer, enabling healthcare providers to select the most appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach. By identifying actionable mutations or protein levels, this testing plays a central role in precision medicine, ensuring that patients receive treatments most likely to be effective while avoiding unnecessary interventions.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

A pathologist is a medical professional and physician expert who specializes in diagnosing diseases, particularly cancer, by examining cells and tissues. They analyze biopsy samples, tissue samples, and other specimens—such as lymph node, bone marrow, and urine samples—under a microscope to detect abnormal cells, confirm the presence of cancer, and determine tumor type, subtype, histology, and grade. This involves comparing cancer cells to normal cells to assess cancer characteristics and assign specific grading systems, such as Gleason patterns for prostate cancer. Pathologists also examine removed tissue to determine cancer stage and test lymph nodes for cancer spread. As part of a multidisciplinary care team, they analyze cells, tissues, and organs removed during biopsies or surgeries, providing essential diagnostic information, staging, and biomarker testing results. They compile their findings into a pathology report, which guides treatment decisions. Their role is critical in confirming cancer diagnoses, identifying tumor subtypes, and evaluating disease progression across various cancer types, including ovarian cancer.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

In all contexts, the Radiation Oncologist's role centers on the expert application of radiation to treat malignant diseases.

The relation (Biopsy, Pathologist) describes the professional interaction and workflow between a biopsy procedure and a pathologist. A biopsy involves the removal of a sample of tissue, such as tumor tissue, from a patient. This sample is subsequently sent to a pathologist, who is a medical specialist responsible for its examination. The pathologist analyzes the cells, tissues, and organs obtained during the biopsy, typically using a microscope, to look for the presence of cancer cells.

The primary purpose of this examination is to confirm whether cancer is present and to reliably diagnose the specific disease. Beyond general cancer detection, the pathologist may also perform specialized assessments, such as assigning Gleason patterns, which are used to grade certain types of cancer. The pathologist’s role is central to the diagnostic process, as their analysis of the biopsy sample provides the definitive information needed to confirm a cancer diagnosis and guide subsequent medical decisions.

entities.description:
Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures of the lymphatic system and integral components of the body’s immune system. Distributed throughout the body, they act as filters for lymph fluid and help fight infection. In the context of cancer, lymph nodes are significant because they can be primary sites of metastasis, where cancer cells spread from a primary tumor. Regional lymph nodes are those located near the tumor, and sentinel lymph nodes are specifically the first nodes to which cancer cells are expected to drain and spread. Cancer involvement in lymph nodes can cause them to swell, and this spread is often detected through imaging techniques such as PET/CT scans, as well as through biopsies. Because they are common sites of metastasis, lymph nodes are frequently biopsied to determine whether cancer has spread, which is a critical step in staging and treatment planning.
Lymph nodes located far from the primary tumor, which can be sites of distant metastasis.
Breast cancer that has spread outside the breast and lymph nodes to other parts of the body.<SEP>Breast cancer that has spread to distant parts of the body, commonly bone and lung.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.
A stage of stomach cancer where the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body, such as the liver, peritoneum, or distant lymph nodes.

Breast Cancer is a disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in breast tissue, most commonly originating in the epithelial cells of the terminal duct lobular units, specifically within the ducts or lobules. The vast majority of breast cancers are carcinomas. This malignant disease can spread to surrounding tissue and other parts of the body, such as the lungs; when it metastasizes, it is still referred to as breast cancer.

The condition is frequently associated with germline mutations, particularly in the BRCA genes, and can be hereditary in approximately 1 out of 10 cases. A personal or family history of breast cancer may also be linked to an increased risk of developing other cancers, such as prostate cancer and thyroid cancer. Clinical discussions of breast cancer often focus on staging, prognostic factors, and the use of biomarker testing and tumor markers for diagnosis and management.

Adrenal glands produce hormones that affect your body in different ways. This chapter reviews the basics of adrenal tumors. Adrenal glands Your body has 2 adrenal glands. They are located on top of each kidney. Adrenal glands are small, yellow glands that are important to the body’s endocrine system. The endocrine system is made up of tissues and organs that produce hormones. Hormones are chemical substances that are made in one part of the body and carried through the bloodstream to other parts of the body where they help control how organs or cells work. Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

Immunotherapy is a form of cancer treatment that leverages the body's own immune system to identify, target, and destroy cancer cells. It is classified as a systemic therapy, meaning it works throughout the body, and functions by either stimulating or re-activating the immune system's natural defenses against tumors. This approach can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments, and its application spans various cancer types, including recurrent ovarian cancer, advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, metastatic thyroid cancer, and primary CNS lymphoma, where the monoclonal antibody rituximab is a key agent.

A prominent and often preferred method within immunotherapy involves the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors, which include drugs that target proteins such as PD-1 and PD-L1. A specific example of this class is pembrolizumab. These inhibitors are frequently utilized in clinical practice, particularly for cancers like metastatic anal cancer, where they serve as a primary treatment or are recommended when the disease progresses during or after chemotherapy. In some cases, such as progressive anal cancer, these inhibitors may be administered before surgery. Additionally, immunotherapy can be delivered directly into the bladder for certain malignancies.

The application of immunotherapy is sometimes guided by the presence of specific biomarkers to determine patient eligibility. While it offers a powerful mechanism for fighting cancer, it is not without side effects. Potential adverse reactions include autoimmune responses, fatigue, fever, nausea, loss of appetite, infection, diarrhea, and constipation. Overall, immunotherapy represents a versatile and increasingly central strategy in oncology, offering options for both early and advanced-stage diseases across a wide spectrum of cancer types.
