Surgery is usually recommended for earlystage cancers, while most locally advanced cancers are treated with chemoradiation. This section applies to the following types of cervical cancer: Squamous cell carcinoma Adenocarcinoma Adenosquamous carcinoma Treatment is based on the cancer stage. The stage describes how far the cancer has likely spread based on imaging and other testing. A risk factor that guides treatment for cervical cancer is lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI). LVSI means that there are tumor cells in the blood vessels or lymph vessels inside the tumor. Cancers with LVSI are more likely to spread to nearby lymph nodes. Nearby lymph nodes are more likely to be removed. Fertility-sparing treatment Surgical treatment for early-stage cervical cancer often involves surgery that removes the uterus (hysterectomy). Carrying a pregnancy is not possible after a hysterectomy. If the cancer has not spread beyond the cervix (stage 1), fertility-sparing treatment may be an option, if desired. This approach involves surgery that does not remove the uterus or ovaries, allowing you the option of natural pregnancy in the future. If fertility-sparing treatment is being considered, ask your doctor about getting the opinion of a reproductive endocrinologist. Reproductive endocrinologists are doctors that specialize in fertility. A fertility-sparing approach is not appropriate for some uncommon types of cervical cancer. Stage 1A1 Cone biopsy is recommended for stage 1A1 cancers without known LVSI. If the results are good, no further treatment is needed. If the results suggest that the cancer was not completely removed, you may have another cone biopsy. Or, your doctor may recommend radical trachelectomy. For stage 1A1 cancers with LVSI, treatment with either cone biopsy or radical trachelectomy is recommended. Pelvic lymph node evaluation should also be performed. If trachelectomy is planned, see the next page for information on treatment after surgery. Stage 1A2 Cone biopsy is an option for some very-lowrisk stage 1A2 cancers. The tumor must be smaller than 2 centimeters, there must be no LVSI, and other criteria must be met. Pelvic lymph node evaluation is performed in addition to the cone biopsy. For stage 1A2 cancers with LVSI, treatment with either cone biopsy or radical trachelectomy is recommended. Pelvic lymph node evaluation is also performed. If trachelectomy is planned, see the next page for information on treatment after surgery. Stage 1B1 Cone biopsy is an option for some very-lowrisk stage 1B1 cancers. The tumor must be smaller than 2 cm, there must be no LVSI, and other criteria must be met. Pelvic lymph node evaluation is also performed. For stage 1B1 cancers that do not meet the criteria for cone biopsy, radical trachelectomy with pelvic lymph node evaluation is recommended. Lymph nodes in the abdomen (para-aortic nodes) may be removed in addition to pelvic lymph nodes. Stage 1B2 Fertility-sparing surgery is not performed often for stage 1B2 cancers. Because most research on fertility-sparing surgery applies to smaller tumors, abdominal surgery is generally preferred. Treatment after surgery If testing finds no cancer in tissue beyond the cervix or in lymph nodes removed during surgery, there are 2 options. External beam radiation therapy (EBRT) is recommended for cancers with risk factors. Observation is recommended for cancers without risk factors. Your doctor will consider the tumor size, whether there is LVSI, and other factors when determining if EBRT is a good choice for you. If EBRT is planned, platinum chemotherapy may be given during the same time period. This is called chemoradiation. If cancer is found in any pelvic or paraaortic lymph nodes, or in any tissues outside the cervix, treatment with chemoradiation is recommended. Vaginal brachytherapy may be given in addition to EBRT and platinum chemotherapy. Fertility-sparing treatment Fertility-sparing treatment may be an option, if desired, for some stage 1 cancers. This approach involves surgery that does not remove the uterus or ovaries, allowing you the option of natural pregnancy in the future. If cancer is found at the margins (edges) of the removed tissue and there is no LVSI, you may or may not have more treatment. If you want the option of becoming pregnant in the future, the cancer can often be observed without treatment. For those who do not want to preserve fertility, an extrafascial (simple) hysterectomy is usually recommended. Surveillance will begin. If cancer or pre-cancer is found in the cone biopsy margins and surgery is not possible, brachytherapy is recommended. EBRT may be given in addition to brachytherapy. If cancer or pre-cancer is found in the cone biopsy margins and surgery is possible, there are two possibilities. Patient is an individual receiving medical care, typically within the context of a suspected or confirmed cancer diagnosis, including specific types such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), mouth cancer, kidney cancer, breast cancer, and bone cancer. This person may be undergoing evaluation, diagnostic testing, medical imaging, and various medical procedures, and is actively engaged with a care team throughout the process. Fertility preservation refers to the range of actions, methods, and processes undertaken to safeguard a person’s ability to have biological children in the future, most commonly discussed and implemented before cancer treatment that may impair fertility. This practice is centered on keeping reproductive options open for later in life, particularly for patients who are at risk of infertility due to medical interventions such as chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. The core objective is to protect or save eggs, sperm, or reproductive tissue so that individuals can potentially conceive biological children after their treatment concludes.

The specific techniques involved in fertility preservation include the collection and freezing of sperm or eggs, as well as more advanced procedures such as ovarian tissue banking and ovarian transposition. These methods are designed to enable future pregnancy by preserving reproductive cells or tissues prior to the start of cancer therapy. The process is typically discussed with patients before they begin treatment, ensuring that they are informed of their options and can make proactive decisions about their reproductive health. While the primary context is cancer care, the underlying principle of fertility preservation is broadly applicable to anyone seeking to maintain the possibility of having children later in life, whether due to medical reasons or personal choice.
An individual diagnosed with cancer.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Patient Portal is an online system or platform designed to give patients access to their personal health information. It enables users to view, download, and retrieve their medical records, including test results, imaging reports, and other health reports. The portal serves as a centralized digital space where patients can review their medical history and stay informed about their health status.

Beyond record access, the Patient Portal facilitates communication between patients and their healthcare providers. It allows patients to track appointments and interact with their care team, supporting ongoing care coordination. The system is intended to empower patients by providing convenient, secure access to their health data and fostering engagement with their own care process.

Mouth Cancer, also known as oral cancer or oral cavity cancer, is a malignant condition that develops in any part of the mouth, including the lips, buccal mucosa (inner cheek lining), tongue, gums, floor of the mouth, hard palate, and retromolar trigone. It is classified as a type of head and neck cancer and most commonly originates in the squamous cells, making it typically a squamous cell carcinoma of the mucosa of the lip and other oral surfaces. The disease is a recognized topic in medical literature and is referenced in resources such as the NCCN (National Comprehensive Cancer Network) guidelines, which provide further information on its management.

Clinically, Mouth Cancer is staged using the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system, with stages ranging from 0 to 4. This staging process is crucial as it directly guides treatment decisions, helping clinicians determine the appropriate therapeutic approach based on the extent of the disease. However, from a molecular perspective, testing for this cancer has limited value due to the scarcity of targeted drugs available for its treatment, which contrasts with other cancer types where molecular profiling may offer more actionable therapeutic options. Overall, Mouth Cancer encompasses a range of malignancies within the oral cavity, with its diagnosis, staging, and treatment protocols being well-documented in oncological practice.

Fertility preservation refers to the range of actions, methods, and processes undertaken to safeguard a person’s ability to have biological children in the future, most commonly discussed and implemented before cancer treatment that may impair fertility. This practice is centered on keeping reproductive options open for later in life, particularly for patients who are at risk of infertility due to medical interventions such as chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. The core objective is to protect or save eggs, sperm, or reproductive tissue so that individuals can potentially conceive biological children after their treatment concludes.

The specific techniques involved in fertility preservation include the collection and freezing of sperm or eggs, as well as more advanced procedures such as ovarian tissue banking and ovarian transposition. These methods are designed to enable future pregnancy by preserving reproductive cells or tissues prior to the start of cancer therapy. The process is typically discussed with patients before they begin treatment, ensuring that they are informed of their options and can make proactive decisions about their reproductive health. While the primary context is cancer care, the underlying principle of fertility preservation is broadly applicable to anyone seeking to maintain the possibility of having children later in life, whether due to medical reasons or personal choice.
Individuals diagnosed with cancer, including those with inflammatory breast cancer, who may experience anxiety and need support.

Head And Neck Cancer is a broad and diverse category of malignancies that arise in the squamous cells lining the mucosal surfaces of the head and neck region. This group encompasses cancers of the oral cavity (including the mouth, jaw, teeth, and gums), the pharynx (throat), the larynx (voice box), and associated glands. As a broader classification, it includes specific subtypes such as throat cancer. The primary risk factors for developing these cancers include the use of tobacco and alcohol, though a subset of these cancers is also caused by the Human Papillomavirus (HPV).

The disease and its treatment can have significant impacts on a patient's quality of life, potentially affecting the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, and may necessitate dental work prior to the initiation of treatment. Furthermore, cancer therapies for this region can impact fertility. For patients, particularly those with smoking or vaping habits, cessation is deemed essential to maximize the chances of a cure and to minimize the severity of treatment-related side effects.

Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

What is primary CNS lymphoma? What causes primary CNS lymphoma? How is primary CNS lymphoma diagnosed? Can primary CNS lymphoma be cured? What’s next? Key points Being diagnosed with a brain tumor can be frightening and overwhelming. This book will help you make sense of all the information that’s out there. It will also describe your options for treatment. Taken together, you’ll have the confidence to make wellinformed decisions. What is primary CNS lymphoma? Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). But people with primary CNS lymphoma often have one or more of these risk factors: Having an immunodeficiency disorder, which is an illness that weakens the immune system’s ability to fight infections and diseases. Primary CNS lymphoma is frequently linked to HIV, the immunodeficiency virus that causes AIDS. Carrying the Epstein-Barr virus, which is the virus that causes mononucleosis (“mono”) and other illnesses. Epstein-Barr is one of the most common viruses in humans. Most people are infected with it. After you’re infected, the virus remains dormant (inactive or “sleeping”) in your body for life. Bone is a specialized connective tissue that forms the skeleton, characterized as a hard yet living tissue composed of bone cells, collagen, blood vessels, nerves, proteins, vitamins, and minerals. It is light and strong, capable of regrowing and undergoing continuous remodeling, and it also produces hormones. As a dynamic tissue, bone can be damaged by cancer, leading to complications such as calcium release into the body.

In the context of oncology, bone is a frequent and clinically significant site for metastasis across multiple cancer types. It is a common site for distant metastasis in breast cancer, including spread to the spine, and is also a primary target for prostate cancer metastasis, often detected via bone scans. Additionally, bone serves as a common site for metastatic esophageal cancer, cervical cancer, liver cancer, and stomach cancer. When cancer spreads to bone, affected areas may appear as bright spots on imaging scans due to increased tracer absorption, indicating active metastatic lesions.
